strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: combining fast one-step real-world super-resolution with optional multi-step inference in one model. The proposed SAD, DTC, and TAR components form a coherent framework. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/ffb5026d146b4063a7d0b244011f405f/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The one-step results are competitive across three benchmarks. TEASR obtains the best reported PSNR/SSIM on DRealSR and DIV2K-Val and strong perceptual scores, including the best LPIPS, DISTS, and FID on RealSR among the compared methods.

Using a shared model to learn real and induced-fake trajectories is potentially useful for scaling distillation, while the branch-wise current/target timestep conditioning is intuitive for conditional consistency training.

The evaluation includes full-reference, perceptual, distributional, and no-reference metrics, along with qualitative comparisons. The authors also acknowledge the fidelity-realism trade-off and the lack of independent control over it.
weaknesses: The central claim that additional sampling steps improve restoration quality is not supported by Table 2. One-step inference is best on PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, and FID; at 30 steps these metrics all deteriorate substantially. Improvements are confined to small, inconsistent changes in no-reference metrics, while MUSIQ is also slightly worse at 30 steps. Thus, variable-step execution is demonstrated, but the claimed useful quality-compute trade-off is not.

The claimed training efficiency is not quantitatively evaluated. Reporting the number of maintained models does not establish memory or computational efficiency across very different backbones. The paper provides no peak-memory, training-time, FLOP, parameter, or matched-baseline measurements. Moreover, the abstract and introduction claim that a 20B-parameter model can be distilled on one A100, whereas Section 4.1 reports training on two A100 GPUs.

The ablations are insufficient to attribute the gains. SAD, the main mechanism, is not ablated; the DTC experiment jointly changes the architecture to a dual branch and decouples the timestep signals; and TAR worsens six of the eight reported metrics relative to DTC without TAR. Its benefit rests mainly on a few qualitative crops. Loss-component, weighting, and stability analyses are absent.

Reproducibility is limited: values or schedules for key loss coefficients are missing, as are crop size/resolution, precise timestep sampling and training staging, detailed degradation settings, memory configuration, and inference latency. The TAR weight w(s)=(1-s)^2/s is singular near zero, but no clipping or numerical treatment is specified.

The comparison does not control for backbone scale or training resources. TEASR uses the very large Qwen-Image backbone, yet no comparable-backbone baseline or parameter-matched study is given. Running other methods with unspecified default prompts/settings further complicates attribution of gains to the proposed method.

The evidence for perceptual superiority is not fully convincing: there is no human preference study, uncertainty across runs, or statistical testing, and several no-reference metrics favor competing methods. The small qualitative selections cannot resolve the disagreement between metrics.

Originality is moderate rather than high because self-adversarial twin trajectories and generalized consistency/shortcut objectives are adapted from recent generation work; the paper does not isolate sufficiently what improvement comes specifically from its Real-ISR modifications.

Presentation and attribution need correction. References contain duplicates, and the cited StableSR reference appears to be an unrelated latent-GAN image-editing paper. Placeholder running headers such as “Abbreviated paper title” and “F. Author et al.” also remain. Overall, the promising one-step results do not compensate for the unsupported and internally inconsistent core efficiency and any-step-quality claims.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: obtaining fast real-world image super-resolution while retaining the option to spend additional inference compute. A unified one-/multi-step model would be useful if convincingly demonstrated.

The combination of self-adversarial distillation, decoupled timestep conditioning, and pixel-space fidelity supervision is technically plausible. Applying single-model self-adversarial flow training to conditional real-world super-resolution has some novelty, although the main ingredients build closely on recent work.
The one-step model is competitive on three benchmarks. It obtains particularly strong LPIPS, DISTS, and FID results on RealSR and strong PSNR/SSIM results on DRealSR and DIV2K-Val.
The evaluation includes several full-reference, perceptual, distributional, and no-reference metrics, comparisons with both one-step and iterative diffusion baselines, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The evidence directly contradicts the central claim that additional sampling steps improve restoration quality. In Table 2, moving from one to 30 steps worsens every full-reference, perceptual, and distributional metric: PSNR 24.83→23.61, SSIM 0.7198→0.6837, LPIPS 0.2542→0.2913, DISTS 0.2003→0.2183, and FID 103.97→118.41. The no-reference changes are small and non-monotonic. A few subjective crops cannot substantiate the claimed quality scalability.

The claimed training efficiency is not actually evaluated. There are no measurements of peak memory, wall-clock training time, throughput, FLOPs, or inference latency. Counting resident models as 1 versus 3 is an inadequate proxy because the proposed method performs multiple passes through a 20B-parameter network and a VAE. Moreover, the abstract claims training on a single A100, whereas the experimental section reports two A100 GPUs.

The comparison confounds the proposed method with a much larger and newer Qwen-Image-2512 backbone. No same-backbone baseline isolates the benefit of SAD, DTC, or TAR, and no comparison establishes that a teacher-based alternative cannot be trained with similar freezing, LoRA, checkpointing, or offloading. Consequently, the reported gains cannot confidently be attributed to the proposed algorithm.

The ablation evidence is weak and partly unfavorable. SAD, the principal contribution, is not ablated at all. Adding TAR to DTC worsens PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, FID, and MANIQA, while improving only MUSIQ and NIQE; nevertheless, it is presented as broadly improving supervision. The qualitative artifact evidence consists of very few selected examples, with no human study, repeated runs, variance estimates, or significance analysis.

The method is insufficiently specified for reproducibility. The manuscript does not provide the complete combined training objective, weights for all constituent losses, training-stage or update schedule, sampling details for the consistency objective, or safeguards for TAR. In particular, w(s)=(1-s)^2/s is singular as s approaches zero under uniform sampling, but no clipping, epsilon, or restricted timestep range is described.

Several technical claims are asserted rather than validated, including that low-noise velocity discrepancies are more reliable, timestep fusion necessarily loses useful information, and DTC causes the benchmark improvements. The paper also does not compare alternative timestep encodings or rectification schedules.

The qualitative figures are too small to reliably judge fine textures and hallucinations, while the real-world evaluation lacks user preference or expert perceptual assessment. Dataset sample counts and uncertainty are not reported, which is especially problematic for FID on potentially small SR benchmarks.

Overall, the work has a promising direction and competitive one-step results, but the two defining claims—better quality with more steps and substantially improved training efficiency—are either contradicted by the presented numbers or unsupported by direct measurements. These are consequential issues rather than minor presentation defects.

strengths: Evaluated as Algorithms/General because no contribution type is declared. The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: obtaining fast real-world super-resolution while retaining a single model that can operate at different sampling budgets.

The unified self-adversarial distillation formulation is appealing. Reusing one model to represent real and fake trajectories could materially reduce the memory burden associated with teacher-student-discriminator pipelines.

The one-step results are strong across RealSR, DRealSR, and DIV2K-Val. TEASR is especially competitive on full-reference and perceptual metrics, including leading LPIPS, DISTS, and FID results on RealSR and strong PSNR/SSIM on DRealSR and DIV2K-Val.

Decoupled timestep conditioning is intuitive and supported by a substantial ablation improvement over the stated baseline. The qualitative examples also suggest good preservation of fine structures and text.

weaknesses: The central claim that quality improves with additional sampling steps is not convincingly supported quantitatively. In Table 2, moving beyond one step worsens PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, and FID; only small, non-monotonic changes occur in the no-reference metrics. The qualitative differences are subtle and lack a human preference study. The claim should be narrowed to a controllable fidelity-realism trade-off unless stronger evidence is provided.

Training efficiency is asserted rather than measured. There are no peak-memory, wall-clock training, throughput, inference-latency, or FLOP comparisons. Counting resident models is an incomplete proxy, especially because TEASR uses a 20B-parameter backbone while baselines may differ substantially in scale. The claim that training is feasible on one A100 also conflicts with the experimental setting reporting two A100 GPUs.

Important implementation details are missing: the flow-matching loss and complete combined objective are not explicitly defined; several loss weights are unspecified; the optimization/staging of the real trajectory, fake trajectory, reconstruction, and rectification objectives is unclear; and no code-release statement is given. These omissions impede reproducibility.

The TAR weight w(s)=(1-s)^2/s is singular as s approaches zero, yet the paper reports sampling s uniformly on [0,1] without specifying clipping, an epsilon, or another stabilization mechanism. This is a material technical omission because near-zero samples can produce unbounded weights.

The ablations do not isolate the main SAD contribution, and TAR worsens most full-reference and distribution metrics relative to DTC alone, including LPIPS and FID. Its benefit is therefore supported mainly by two no-reference metrics and a small qualitative comparison. More complete loss-component, weighting-function, and training-stability ablations are needed.

Benchmark reliability is difficult to assess because dataset sample counts, evaluation resolution/preprocessing, random-seed treatment, confidence intervals, and repeated-run variance are not reported. FID in particular can be unstable on small evaluation sets. Fairness across baselines with different backbones, training data, and default prompts/settings also needs more careful accounting.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: combining one-step super-resolution with the option to spend additional inference compute, while avoiding separate teacher and discriminator networks.

The proposed framework is technically coherent. Self-adversarial distillation, decoupled timestep conditioning, and the rectification weighting are described with equations, pseudocode, and a supplementary derivation.

The one-step model is competitive across three benchmarks and eight metrics. Particularly strong results include PSNR/SSIM on DRealSR and several perceptual or distributional metrics on RealSR and DIV2K-Val.
The experiments include comparisons with both one-step and iterative methods, component ablations, memory and latency measurements, training curves, and numerous qualitative examples.

The supplementary material exposes useful implementation details and acknowledges trade-offs between fidelity and perceptual realism. weaknesses: The central claim that quality improves with additional sampling steps is not supported by Table 3. From one to 30 steps, PSNR falls from 24.83 to 23.61, SSIM from 0.7198 to 0.6837, while LPIPS, DISTS, and FID all worsen. NIQE improves, but MUSIQ and MANIQA do not show a consistent trend. Selected visual examples are insufficient to establish an overall quality improvement without a controlled human study.

The main quality comparison is strongly confounded by backbone scale: TEASR uses a 20B-parameter Qwen-Image model, whereas reported competitors use much smaller backbones. The same-backbone Z-Image experiment reports memory and a few images but no benchmark accuracy, so it does not isolate the proposed algorithm's benefit from that of the stronger prior.

The efficiency framing is incomplete and occasionally contradictory. The paper says that a 20B model can be distilled on one A100, but the reported full training uses two A100s. TEASR also consumes 77.69 GB during training and 59.19 GB during inference, versus 22.87 GB training memory and 5.93 GB inference memory for OSEDiff. Thus it is efficient in relative overhead and model count, but not in absolute resources or latency.

The ablations do not convincingly validate all components. SAD is not ablated, despite being the central contribution. Adding TAR to DTC worsens PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, and FID; its benefit rests on some no-reference metrics and an informal claim of fewer checkerboard artifacts, without quantitative artifact analysis or human evaluation.

Several reproducibility details are missing or unclear, including the LPIPS loss weight, exact evaluation preprocessing and sample counts, random-seed variability, and sufficiently detailed implementations of the DMD/ADD comparisons in Figure 5. The abstract also contains an empty code link.

The originality is moderate: self-adversarial twin trajectories are inherited from recent generation work, the dual-branch conditioning follows OminiControl, and the TAR weight follows the standard flow-matching score/KL relation. Stronger controlled evidence is needed to demonstrate that their combination constitutes a substantial advance for super-resolution.

There are presentation and attribution issues, including an apparently incorrect reference for StableSR and claims such as “consistently outperforms” or “superior performance” that are broader than the mixed metric results justify. Overall, the method is promising, but the evidence currently gives a slight preference for rejection under the default Algorithms/General contribution type.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: reducing diffusion-based real-world super-resolution sampling cost while retaining flexibility in the number of inference steps.

The single-model self-adversarial formulation is practically appealing. Encoding real and fake trajectories through different target-timestep conditions avoids maintaining separate teacher and discriminator networks.

The one-step model is quantitatively competitive: it obtains the best LPIPS, DISTS, and FID on RealSR; strong fidelity and perceptual results on DRealSR; and the best PSNR/SSIM on DIV2K-Val among the reported methods.

The experiments cover three benchmarks, several full-reference and no-reference metrics, qualitative comparisons, memory measurements, sampling-step analysis, and some ablations. Fine-tuning a 20B-parameter backbone with a reported 15.6% memory increase over its LoRA baseline is noteworthy.
weaknesses: The central claim that additional sampling steps improve restoration quality is contradicted by Table 3. From 1 to 30 steps, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, and FID all deteriorate. MUSIQ and MANIQA fluctuate and are not better at 30 steps, leaving only NIQE with a consistent favorable change. The qualitative assertion of more natural details cannot support the paper's broad 'quality scalability' claim without a controlled human study.

The comparison does not isolate the proposed method from backbone scale. TEASR uses a 20B Qwen-Image backbone, whereas the principal baselines use 0.8B–2B models. The Z-Image experiment reports memory and a few qualitative examples but no benchmark accuracy or same-backbone comparison. Consequently, the gains cannot be confidently attributed to SAD, DTC, or TAR.

The TAR evidence is unconvincing. Relative to DTC without TAR, adding TAR worsens PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, and FID; its support rests mainly on two no-reference metrics and a small qualitative claim about checkerboard artifacts. No human evaluation or statistical analysis establishes that this trade-off is preferable.

The theoretical derivation is internally inconsistent. Given the paper's interpolation z_s=(1-s)x+sε and velocity target ε−x, the score relation in supplementary Eq. 7 has the wrong sign on the velocity term. Moreover, the displayed expression in Eq. 10 does not algebraically imply Eq. 11. Although the final weighting magnitude may be recoverable with a corrected derivation, the presented justification for TAR is not sound.

Ablation coverage is insufficient for the main claims. SAD, the foundation of the method, is explicitly not ablated; there is no comparison against ordinary consistency training or a separate-model DMD alternative under matched conditions; and the DTC baseline is not specified sufficiently to determine whether the gain comes from timestep decoupling, the dual-branch architecture, or another implementation difference.

The efficiency framing is overstated. TEASR requires about 59 GB for one-step inference and 0.72 seconds per image, versus 5.9 GB and 0.15 seconds for OSEDiff. Training uses 77.69 GB and the reported main run uses two A100 GPUs, despite repeated emphasis on single-GPU feasibility. Counting maintained models or relative overhead alone does not establish practical efficiency.

Reproducibility details contain inconsistencies: the main paper reports batch size 1 with gradient accumulation 2, while the supplement reports batch size 4 with gradient accumulation 2; the code field is blank; and important settings such as the LPIPS weight, exact evaluation protocol, seeds, uncertainty, and sufficiently precise baseline configuration are missing. Overall, the manuscript has a promising one-model idea and strong one-step numbers, but the unsupported any-step claim, confounded comparisons, inadequate ablations, and flawed derivation are consequential shortcomings. strengths: Under the default Algorithms/General framing, TEASR offers a practically meaningful contribution: one diffusion model supports one-, few-, and multi-step real-world super-resolution without auxiliary teacher or discriminator networks.

The self-adversarial distillation formulation is technically interesting, and the decoupled timestep conditioning is a sensible architectural response to the two-time conditioning required by consistency-style training.

The one-step results are competitive across RealSR, DRealSR, and DIV2K-Val. TEASR achieves particularly strong LPIPS, DISTS, and FID on RealSR and strong PSNR/SSIM on DRealSR and DIV2K-Val, despite using only one maintained model.

Training-efficiency evidence is encouraging. On the controlled Z-Image-6B comparison, TEASR substantially reduces memory relative to DMD and ADD, while the Qwen-Image experiment demonstrates feasibility with a 20B-parameter backbone.

The paper evaluates numerous fidelity, perceptual, distributional, and no-reference metrics, includes qualitative comparisons and sensitivity analysis, and provides a reasonably detailed training algorithm and theoretical motivation for TAR.
weaknesses: The central claim that quality improves as sampling steps increase is not convincingly supported quantitatively. From 1 to 30 steps, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, and FID all worsen on RealSR; MUSIQ and MANIQA are nearly flat or non-monotonic, with only NIQE improving consistently. The evidence supports a changing fidelity-realism trade-off more clearly than a general quality improvement.

TAR is weakly validated. Relative to DTC without TAR, it worsens PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, and FID, while improving mainly MUSIQ and NIQE. The claimed removal of checkerboard artifacts rests on limited qualitative examples and no human study, artifact metric, or evaluation across multiple datasets.

The any-step evaluation is incomplete: quantitative step-scaling results are reported only on RealSR, and there is no systematic comparison against competing methods operated at matched step counts, latency, or compute. Thus, superiority of the multi-step mode remains uncertain.

Efficiency comparisons require more careful qualification. The absolute Qwen-based inference cost is high—about 59 GB and 0.72 seconds even for one step versus 5.9 GB and 0.15 seconds for OSEDiff—and comparisons across different backbone sizes conflate framework efficiency with model scale. The claim of training the 20B model on a single GPU is also not demonstrated by the reported main experiment, which uses two A100 GPUs, although the measured memory reportedly fits one 80 GB A100.

Some reproducibility details are missing or inconsistent: the code field is empty; the LPIPS loss coefficient, crop and augmentation settings, and evaluation sample details are unspecified; and the main text samples TAR time over U(0,1), where its weight is singular near zero, whereas the supplementary algorithm uses U(0.05,0.95). Results also lack repeated-run variability.

Novelty is partly incremental relative to prior self-adversarial flow distillation: the principal advance is its adaptation to real-world super-resolution plus DTC and TAR. Given the mixed TAR evidence and limited multi-step evaluation, the scientific case is promising but not yet fully convincing.
